title: Chapter 127 — Email & Written Communication
intro: Every email you send is a permanent record of your professionalism.

sections.title: Email Standards
sections.content:
Response time is a promise. Within 4 hours during business hours — that is the standard. Every hour past that, the customer wonders if you care.

Subject lines should be clear and specific — 'Your Bosch dishwasher quote — valid through Friday' not 'Following up.' The customer has 50 emails in their inbox. Yours needs to stand out for the right reasons.

Lead with the action item or answer. The first sentence should tell them why you are writing. Do not bury the point under three sentences of pleasantries. Use their name. Keep it concise. End with a clear next step.

Proofread everything. One typo in a $10,000 quote makes you look careless. A model number error costs real money — wrong product ordered, wrong product delivered, complaint, return. Read every email twice before sending — especially the ones with numbers, model numbers, and prices.

sections.title: Tone in Writing
sections.content:
Write with a professional tone without sounding robotic. 'Hi Sarah, great talking with you today' is better than 'Dear Ms. Smith, per our discussion.' Match the customer's tone — if they write casually, respond casually. If they write formally, mirror that.

When handling complaints in writing, never match anger. A calm, solution-focused email defuses more tension than a defensive one. 'I understand your frustration about the delivery delay. Here is what I am doing to fix it right now.' That sentence does three things: acknowledges the emotion, takes ownership, and promises action.

Avoid passive voice in complaint responses. Not 'the delivery was delayed' but 'we delayed your delivery and I apologize.' Active voice shows ownership. Passive voice sounds like you are hiding behind process.

sections.title: Know When to Call Instead
sections.content:
Some conversations should not happen over email. Bad news — call. Complaints — call. Complex technical discussions — call. Anything where tone could be misread — call.

Email is for information delivery: confirmations, quote PDFs, follow-up summaries, and scheduling. Phone is for relationship-building, problem-solving, and anything emotionally charged. Text is for quick updates and time-sensitive logistics.

The golden rule of written communication: every message should either answer a question, provide information, or give them a reason to respond. If it does none of those three things, do not send it. Unnecessary emails train customers to stop reading your messages.
